summary: Native read-only review of artifact digest 2c189ad0a6c54769e0f5c3904757a4a14a46add1a1e021e9327a9ff3ab733511 is changes-required. The corrected artifacts now cover bounded nonreflecting device bodies, opaque owner/source-session failures, grant expiry and OFF-independent cleanup, purge/export exclusion, directory durability, protected credential storage, explicit operation consent, and provider-neutral browser authorization. No implicit consent or second Google/Apple authentication provider was found. However, the newly fetched shared-auth dependency at origin/feat/modern-auth@bc7fc72c35b7bf794eff912c07bdd38a1d1f0816 establishes an accepted single transactional SQLite Identity authority. The frozen JSON-grant/file-lock design cannot preserve that authority or provider-linked session revocation. The CLI ADR also collides with the accepted ADR-0028 identifier. These are implementer-owned compatibility corrections; no product decision is required. This review is correlated and unverified, with no executable, shell-reviewer, or adapter provenance asserted, and it does not claim that the dependency has landed on main or that implementation was reviewed.

findings.category: Identity authority, atomic issuance, and provider revocation
findings.description: The frozen device authorization design persists grants in JSON and coordinates them with sessions through a new process/file lock. The accepted modern-auth dependency instead makes auth.sqlite3 the sole Identity authority and requires proof consumption, fresh account/session/auth-version checks, and session issuance in one transaction. Its session rows carry auth_version, auth_method, and provider_binding_id, and provider revocation deletes sessions by binding. The proposed file lock is not observed by AuthStore transactions, while the CLI contract does not preserve the approving session's provider/version lineage. Consequently an exchange can race an auth-version change or provider unlink/revocation, and a newly issued CLI session can survive loss of the provider authority that approved it. This is an authorization and revocation hole, not merely an architecture preference.

findings.recommendation: Reconcile the CLI authorization contract with the accepted modern Identity authority before implementation. Device grants must live under AuthStore with their bounded retention, purge, and export exclusion; approval/exchange must conditionally consume the grant and insert the CLI session in the same AuthStore transaction after fresh source-session, owner, deletion, auth_version, exposure, expiry, and provider-binding checks. Preserve the approving session's auth_version, auth_method, and provider_binding_id revocation lineage, or an equivalent binding enforced by the same transaction and foreign keys. Remove the independent JSON authority and flock design. Add deterministic races for provider unlink/revocation, auth-version changes, password reset, logout, and purge versus exchange.

findings.category: Accepted ADR compatibility and review binding
findings.description: The frozen plan requires acceptance of a proposed ADR-0028 for CLI authorization, but the shared-auth dependency already contains accepted ADR-0028 for the single Identity authority. The two records make incompatible persistence decisions and cannot share an identifier. The generic instruction to reconcile shared-auth before candidate freeze does not resolve the current reviewed contract, source-hash binding, or rollback assumptions.
